newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity's Pozen says staunching manager exodus.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity's Pozen says staunching manager exodus.

text.p: The new president and chief executive officer of Fidelity Management and Research Co, the investment advisor to the nation's largest family of mutual funds, said on Monday he is in the process of staunching the exodus of portfolio managers from the privately-held company.
"We are in the baseline of doing that now," said Robert Pozen, who moves up from being the general counsel for the company that manages nearly $500 billion in assets.

"We've bit the bullet and made the tough decisions last year in the equity group. We now have people well positioned. We've reviewed the comp(ensation) systems and what we're really going to do is keep the themes of continuity and stability," Pozen said.

The 50-year-old Pozen made his remarks after Fidelity confirmed that Bart Grenier, 38, the assistant head of the firm's stock division and former research chief, was leaving. Some 25 portfolio managers, including Jeff Vinik and Brian Posner, have left Fidelity in the last 18 months to land jobs at competitors.
"There will always be some defections. There's no way you can stop that," Pozen said.

A lawyer with no specific investing background, Pozen said, "Think about what this job is from a functional role...this is a management job. It involves going down the organization managing personnel, reviewing performance, designing appropriate comp(ensation) systems, providing technology support. These are all things that I've been very involved with at Fidelity before."
He said the job comes down to "being a good people manager and really knowing how to work the Fidelity organization and make things happen. That's what these people need."

But Alpha Equity Research's David O'Leary, a Fidelity watcher, said Pozen's legal background "will increase the friction with the star portfolio and probably accelerate defections in the coming weeks."
"This change creates a wide gap between senior management and portfolio managers that could have a negative impact on Fidelity's future growth and performance," O'Leary said.

Pozen, who has been with Fidelity for 10 years, told Reuters he had also advised people in Washington that he was no longer interested in any government positions. As recently as April 7, he had been rumored to be the next deputy U.S. Trade Representative in charge of Asia.
Pozen takes Gary Burkhead's job and Burkhead is moving up to vice chairman of FMR Corp, Fidelity's parent company, with responsibility for Fidelity's institutional business.
During Burkhead's tenure as chief investment officer, Fidelity's assets under management rose from about $50 billion to almost $500 billion.

But O'Leary said Fidelity funds as a group underperformed some other mutual funds. He said the Vanguard S&P 500 fund was up 86 percent over the last three years, but noted that Fidelity's Growth and Income Fund was up 75 percent, Fidelity's ContraFund was up 65 percent and Magellan, the nation's largest mutual fund, was up 55 percent for the same period.
